entries.title: Man runs red light, causes two buses to crash: police
entries.summary: <p>A bus driver was in critical condition and at least eight other people were hospitalized after a driver ran a red light and caused two CTA buses to crash in East Garfield Park Wednesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>A man driving a sedan eastbound on West Lake Street at 6:42 p.m. drove through a red light and hit a CTA bus going south on South Homan Avenue, which then hit another CTA bus going north on Homan, police said. The driver of the second CTA bus was taken to Stroger Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>The driver of the sedan was issued several citations and also taken to Stroger Hospital, in stable condition, police said. Seven bus passengers also were taken to local hospitals in various conditions.</p><p>The CTA didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.</p>

entries.title: Teen charged in fatal Back of the Yards shooting
entries.summary: <p>A teen was arrested and charged Tuesday in the fatal shooting of a man in Back of the Yards last August, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The 17-year-old faces a charge of first-degree murder, police said. He was arrested in Hickory Hills on Tuesday.</p><p>David Carmona, 20, was arguing with someone in the 4700 block of South Damen Avenue when he turned to walk away, and other person allegedly shot him in the buttocks, police said. Carmona was taken in critical condition to Stroger Hospital, where he later died.</p>

entries.title: Marina Mabrey and the Sky still see the best in each other
entries.summary: <p>There are many ways to identify former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> guard Marina Mabrey. She's a middle child. One of the best players in the league to have never been named an All-Star. Inventor of the "Crash-Out Jar," a running joke in which she deposited dollars after losing her temper in games.</p><p></p><p>Now, add "face of the franchise" to the list.</p><p></p><p>The Tempo signed her to a two-year max contract this past offseason, making her and Brittney Sykes the faces of the league's first Canadian team.</p><p></p><p>She led the Tempo to an 111-104 win over the Sky Wednesday night, scoring 23 points on 9-13 from the field — and almost immediately reminding fans that the Mabrey experience contains multitudes.</p><p></p><p>Step-back threes. Incredulous conversations with the officials. Perfectly-timed floaters. Poorly-timed fouls.</p><p></p><p>Mabrey's brief tenure with the Sky contained multitudes too. She set the single-season record for three pointers in 2023 (81) and grew her game in 2024. But<b> </b>her stint ended in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky-and-wnba/2024/07/19/marina-mabreys-trade-request-came-with-a-desire-to-play-for-sun" target="_blank" >a request to be traded</a>from the Sky to the Sun midway through the 2024 season. At shootaround before the game, she reflected on how those experiences shaped her.</p><p></p><p>"I've been in leadership positions in Chicago and Connecticut where there were some things I still needed to learn, and I'm still learning right now, but I think that I took those things and put it into this team," Mabrey told the Sun-Times.</p><p></p><p>"I think finding a home helps a lot too. I've jumped around trying to find a situation that works for me and my vision for myself."</p><p></p><p>The Tempo are Mabrey’s fourth team in six years. She's moved from Dallas to Chicago to Connecticut, now to Toronto, all before the age of 30.</p><p></p><p>Few have cycled through as many situations as Mabrey has. Except, perhaps, for the Sky.</p><p></p><p>Mabrey saw the organizational chaos firsthand, living through the peak instability of Chicago's post-2021 championship era. Coach and general manager James Wade, who brought her to Chicago, left in the middle of the 2023 season. Then franchise pillar Kahleah Copper requested a trade.</p><p></p><p>The lesson she took was about staying true to herself.</p><p></p><p>"I think knowing that people will come in and out of organizations, you will have different people to work with, but keeping the vision for yourself that you know is you," she said. "Regardless of who you're playing around, who's coming in, who's not coming in, who's leaving.</p><p></p><p>"I think for me, I maybe lost myself a little bit in Chicago, in trying to figure out who I was alongside everyone. ... I lost the vision of who I know I can be."</p><p></p><p>According to Sykes, who has played against Mabrey since childhood, her vision is to become an offensive juggernaut — but one who has learned to wield her emotions rather than be consumed by them.</p><p></p><p>That's something Tempo coach Sandy Brondello, a two-time WNBA champion, is trying to facilitate.</p><p></p><p>"She's actually quite funny," Brondello said of Mabrey. "Now, if she crashes out, it's usually at the officials. It's never at her teammates, which is a good thing. Now it's more like, 'Just don't get too high or too low.'</p><p></p><p>"But that's her edge. You don't want to change someone. That's her competitive fire. But not letting it affect her overall game."</p><p></p><p>Mabrey only played in Chicago from 2023-2024, but she left a mark on the organization. She embodies two of their defining characteristics: a willingness to risk draft capital to win now, and a spotty track record in retaining stars.</p><p></p><p>To acquire her from the Wings, Wade traded away a staggering amount of draft capital: a 2023 first-rounder, a 2024 first-rounder and a 2025 pick swap.</p><p></p><p>It set the tone for a philosophy that current general manager Jeff Pagliocca has maintained. In Chicago, there will be no tanking, no waiting to strike gold in the draft lottery. Every year it's trying to bring in the best players through trades and free agency, at pretty much whatever cost.</p><p></p><p>So far, the strategy hasn't yielded a ton of tangible success — the Sky have missed the postseason the last two years — but it also hasn't backfired to the proportions one might have imagined.</p><p></p><p>The Mabrey deal is a perfect example. The 2023 pick the Sky surrendered ultimately became a worthless late first-rounder, and the 2025 swap was canceled entirely when the Wings won the No. 1 pick on their own. Had the Sky been able to retain Mabrey, the trade could have aged as a win.</p><p></p><p>She is now producing at the level Wade likely envisioned — 18.8 points per game — and that current coach Tyler Marsh respects.</p><p></p><p>His keys for success against the Tempo revolved around keeping Mabrey in vision at all times, given how quickly she gets off her shot.</p><p></p><p>"I'm a big fan of Marina, the toughness and competitiveness that she plays with — you accept some other stuff that comes with it," Marsh said. "I remember when we played Connecticut last year and I got thrown out of that game, I saw Marina after the game, I said, 'I pulled a you tonight.'"</p><p></p><p>The respect goes both ways.</p><p></p><p>Mabrey is genuinely impressed with the direction the Sky roster has gone. She said at shootaround that Pagliocca has built a tougher and more talented roster — two of his primary goals.</p><p></p><p>Despite all the turbulence, it appears both sides can still see the best in each other.</p>

entries.title: DOJ investigation referred E. Jean Carroll for prosecution in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The Justice Department earlier this year referred an investigation into E. Jean Carroll, the longtime advice columnist who accused President Donald Trump of sexual assault, to federal prosecutors in Chicago, a law enforcement source told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>That investigation is active within U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office, the source said. </p><p>Neither the U.S. Department of Justice nor Boutros' office immediately responded to requests for comment Wednesday night. The story was first reported by <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/05/27/politics/exclusive-justice-department-launched-e-jean-carroll-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>CNN</u></a>.</p><p>Prosecutors are focused on a 2022 deposition by Carroll in which she said she received no outside funding for her legal action against Trump, though it was later revealed that billionaire LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman had chipped in for some legal fees and expenses, CNN reported. Hoffman has a nonprofit based in Chicago.</p><p>In January 2024, as Trump closed in on the Republican presidential nomination, a jury awarded $83.3 million to Carroll in that same suit for Trump’s continued social media attacks against her over her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/6/21/18701574/e-jean-carroll-donald-trump-rape" target="_blank" ><u>claims that he sexually assaulted her</u></a> in a Manhattan department store. That total includes a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/9/23717528/jury-finds-trump-liable-for-sexual-abuse-awards-accuser-e-jean-carroll-5-million" target="_blank" ><u>$5 million sexual abuse and defamation verdict</u></a> in May 2023 she was awarded by another jury.</p><p>The jury that issued the May 2023 verdict rejected Carroll’s claim that she was raped, finding Trump responsible for a lesser degree of sexual abuse. The judgment offered vindication to Carroll, whose allegations had been mocked and dismissed by Trump for years.</p><p>Trump has since appealed the awards multiple times, including to the Supreme Court, which has <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-carroll-abuse-defamation-670dd7ed241e22c52bd16e82a9febf69" target="_blank" ><u>repeatedly rejected</u></a> the president’s requests to hear the case.</p><p>It comes at a time when Boutros’ office is embroiled in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/27/broadview-six-boutros-kat-abughazaleh-ice-trump-chicago-broadview" target="_blank" ><u>biggest credibility crisis it has faced in recent memory</u></a>.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” case against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" ><u>fell apart days before trial</u></a> after a judge discovered improprieties during grand jury proceedings.</p><p>The alleged misconduct by prosecutors came to light only after a lengthy push by defense attorneys to get the judge to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/04/broadview-six-grand-jury-transcript-conspiracy" target="_blank" ><u>review unredacted transcripts</u></a> of what occurred, and shockwaves from the case have begun to reach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/27/broadview-six-boutros-kat-abughazaleh-ice-trump-chicago-broadview" target="_blank" entries.title: Twins manager Derek Shelton not surprised by White Sox' strong play
entries.summary: <p><b>Derek Shelton</b>, who grew up in north suburban Gurnee, is grateful for a second chance to manage in the majors with the Twins. And he’s with another club that plays in the same division as a Chicago team.</p><p>Starting in 2020, Shelton spent five-plus seasons guiding the Pirates — one of the Cubs’ rivals in the National League Central — until they dismissed him last May after a 12-26 start.</p><p>In his return to the Twins, for whom he was a bench coach in 2018 and 2019, Shelton said he isn’t surprised his team is chasing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> in the American League Central, even if the South Siders are coming off three seasons with 101 or more losses. After the second-place Sox’ 15-2 rout Wednesday, the Twins trail them by 1½ games.</p><p>‘‘I don’t think it’s surprising at all,’’ Shelton, 55, said of the Sox’ climb. ‘‘I think [general manager] <b>Chris</b> [<b>Getz</b>] and [assistant GM] <b>Josh Barfield</b> and [manager] <b>Will Venable</b> have done an unbelievable job. I mean, they’ve put a plan in place and stuck to that plan.</p><p>‘‘You know, they went out and made really good signings. When you get a first baseman of this caliber [<b>Munetaka Murakami</b>], they got [starter <b>Anthony</b>] <b>Kay</b>, [<b>Colson</b>] <b>Montgomery</b> is a really good player, [<b>Miguel</b>] <b>Vargas</b> they traded for — this is a good baseball team.’’</p><p>In his second managerial job, Shelton said he’s paying attention to detail more than ever.</p><p>‘‘I do think that one of the things that came out of last year was I thought I got away from the attention to detail, what I thought was the attention to detail from my space,’’ he said. ‘‘I wanted to make sure that if I ever did get the next opportunity that I would stay more on top of it and that I would build a staff that stays on top of it.’’</p><p>Shelton was a standout catcher at Warren Township High School, where he was coached by his dad, <b>Ron</b>. He then went on to play at Southern Illinois and in the minors before turning to coaching and, ultimately, managing.</p><p>He said he doesn’t think anyone can be fully prepared for his first managerial job in the majors.</p><p>‘‘The first year you manage, you’re drinking from the fire hose,’’ said Shelton, noting that 2020 was the COVID-shortened season with extra regulations. ‘‘I didn’t know what I was doing.’’</p><h3>Swiss Army knife, made in Japan?</h3><p>Twins left-hander <b>Connor Prielipp</b> started Wednesday, so right-handed-hitting <b>Randal Grichuk</b> took over in right field and batted cleanup, contributing three hits and two RBI in an 18-hit attack. That gave left-handed-hitting newcomer <b>Rikuu Nishida</b> his first day off in the majors after two eventful games.</p><p>Nishida, who played mostly at second base in the minors, admitted that getting used to right field in a major-league stadium presented him with some challenges, even if he made some nifty catches and threw out two runners at the plate.</p><p>Venable said he is confident the 5-6, 150-pound Nishida will excel in right or anywhere else.</p><p>‘‘He’s a baseball player, kind of like [<b>Sam</b>] <b>Antonacci</b>, where you feel like you can throw him anywhere and he’ll make the adjustments and get the job done,’’ Venable said.</p><h3>Hays’ day off</h3><p>Venable said outfielder <b>Austin Hays</b> is being held back by ‘‘lower-body soreness’’ and took Wednesday off during his rehab assignment with Triple-A Charlotte for a strained left calf.</p><p>Hays missed most of April because of a strained right hamstring. entries.title: Jameson Taillon allows two more home runs, but he sees some positives
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH — Two home runs, one coming on a fastball that clipped the high outside corner, one coming on a fastball that clipped the low inside corner.</p><p>Those home runs — a three-run shot by <b>Brandon Lowe</b> that wiped out an early 3-0 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> advantage and a solo shot by rookie <b>Konnor Griffin</b> that erased a 4-3 Cubs lead — will form the narrative around <b>Jameson Taillon’s</b> latest start.</p><p>He understands that. He knows that he has allowed a major-league-leading 19 home runs, four more than <b>Zack Littell</b> of the Nationals. He knows, after allowing four runs to the Pirates in five innings Wednesday night at PNC Park, that the ERA sits at 5.37 11 starts in.</p><p>He’s not oblivious to the grumbling back home. But where others measure steep decline, and Taillon, 34, acknowledges that he has to keep the ball in the yard, he insists that if you look hard enough, you will see some positives, too. Taillon sees a better shape to his pitches, a slight uptick in velocity, room to mix up his repertoire so he isn’t as predictable.</p><p>“It’s just, unfortunately, my time to go through it right now, but I feel great,’’ he said. “I’m really encouraged by what I’m doing and the work I’m doing. But I’ll keep saying it: I’m really excited about the long term, really upset about the short term.’’</p><h3>PCA tormentor</h3><p>Pirates first baseman <b>Spencer Horwitz </b>smiled when he was told that <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> said he might have won Horwitz the Gold Glove by hitting three rockets that he turned into outs Monday night.</p><p>Horwitz snagged two line drives and a wicked one-hop smash, all with exit velocities of 100-plus mph.</p><p>The line drives, Horwitz said, were pretty much hit right at him.</p><p>“A little jump, that was it,’’ he said. ‘‘The third one, the grounder, a one-hopper, that was a top-spinner that went to my left. I’ve been working really hard on my first-step quickness, a drop step. We’re going to get it in, and I think it showed there.’’</p><p>Horwitz appreciated the compliment from PCA, but doesn’t foresee any Gold Gloves, at least not any time soon. Did he have any message to impart to PCA?</p><p>He smiled again.</p><p>“Maybe try bunting,’’ he said.</p><h3>For me and my Al</h3><p>Hall of Fame broadcaster <b>Pat Hughes</b>, in his 31st season of calling Cubs games on the radio, turned 71 on Wednesday. Hughes, who began his broadcasting career as a 22-year-old calling minor-league baseball in San Jose in 1978, shared a story from his days broadcasting Marquette basketball with Marquette’s motorcycle-riding legendary coach, <b>Al McGuire</b>.</p><p>“We had a game in Charlotte one night, and that day, as I was preparing, my wife called,’’ Hughes recalled.</p><p>“ ‘Pat, I just got a strange call from Al McGuire. He said, ‘Hi, honey, it’s Al. Is Pat there?’ I said, ‘No, he’s in Charlotte.’</p><p>“He says, ‘Oh, that’s where I’m supposed to be! Thanks.’</p><p>“Al shows up at around 5:30. Tipoff is 7. He looks like he hasn’t shaved in a week. He’s wearing a sweatsuit and carrying his suit over his shoulder. I said, ‘We’re taping the pregame show in about 10 minutes.’ He said, ‘Don’t worry, I’ll be there.’</p><p>‘‘So he disappears into the UNC-Charlotte locker room, grabs a student assistant who is thrilled to be talking to the great Al McGuire, and while Al is changing, he gives him a rundown on the whole team.’</p><p>“We begin the taping and I say, ‘Al, this Charlotte team is going to pose a real challenge.’ And he says, ‘Oh, Charlotte, here are their best shooters, the guys who play the best defense, the guys you don’t want to foul late’ as if he’d been preparing all day.’’</p><p>McGuire entries.title: White Sox' David Sandlin brilliant in major-league debut — and he gets plenty of support
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> turned to fireballing right-hander David Sandlin to start — and to make his major-league debut — Wednesday against the American League Central rival Twins.</p><p>The script couldn’t have gone better, save for one early blip in the Sox’ 15-2 victory.</p><p>The 6-4, 220-pound Sandlin yielded a 417-foot home run to Twins leadoff man Byron Buxton on his second pitch, a low but center-cut 97.2 mph four-seam fastball that quickly cleared the fence in left-center field. Buxton raced around the bases after his 17th homer produced a quick 1-0 lead for the Twins.</p><p>‘‘I feel like that kind of took the weight off, almost,’’ Sandlin said. ‘‘I was like, ‘Man, it can’t get worse than that,’ you know? Like, ‘Let’s go now. Welcome to it,’ I guess.’’</p><p>What a welcome it was for Sandlin, 25, who settled in sensationally to stymie any more celebrations. He retired the next 18 hitters in a row, the most by any Sox pitcher in his big-league debut in the last 100 years, according to Elias.</p><p>Sandlin exited after six innings, having thrown only 61 pitches, 41 of them for strikes. He said couldn’t remember dealing the kind of run he dished out against the Twins.</p><p>‘‘I feel like when I pitch best, my mind kind of goes blank and [it’s] just muscle memory out there,’’ Sandlin said.</p><p>He allowed only the one hit, struck out four and walked none before manager Will Venable called on reliever Brandon Eisert to start the seventh.</p><p>‘‘Of course, I tried to get one more [inning],’’ Sandlin said. ‘‘But I knew, like, it was it after [Venable] talked to me. But after that, it was just a surreal feeling.’’</p><p>Meanwhile, the Sox backed Sandlin with an 18-hit attack and their highest run output in three years to give him his first victory.</p><p>Chase Meidroth hit his first career grand slam in the seventh. Munetaka Murakami followed with an opposite-field shot to left to join Jim Thome and Frank Thomas as the only Sox players to reach 20 homers before June.</p><p>Murakami has gone deep in three consecutive games is tied for the American League lead in homers with the Astros’ Yordan Alvarez. He also stole his first base in the majors, taking second standing up in the sixth.</p><p>Randal Grichuk added three hits and two RBI, and Sam Antonacci had his first three-hit game in the majors.</p><p>The rout started when Antonacci singled off Twins starter Connor Prielipp’s glove on a crazy, up-the-middle bouncer to drive in two runs in the second. Colson Montgomery lined an RBI double to the wall in left-center in the third, plating Miguel Vargas.</p><p>The Sox added five more runs in the fifth to boost their lead to 8-1. Grichuk drove in the first run of the inning with an RBI single, and Edgar Quero followed with a sacrifice fly. Two more runs scored on a single by Luisangel Acuna and a bad relay throw. Grichuk drove in another run in the sixth to make it 9-1.</p><p>Sandlin, who was called up from Triple-A Charlotte on Tuesday, kept to his promise of using his heater and ‘‘getting after people with it,’’ reaching a velocity up to 99.3 mph.</p><p>Against the Twins, Sandlin mixed other pitches into his repertoire, including a cutter, sweeper, curve and changeup across a variety of speeds.</p><p>‘‘Just incredible,’’ Venable said. ‘‘He was effective in the zone with all his pitches. There was some swing-and-miss there, gave up a lot of fly balls. Some really good plays defensively throughout the game, but he was just attacking the zone in every way he wanted to.</p><p>‘‘He really pitched with an edge. entries.title: Timely home runs help Cubs end 10-game losing streak
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH — At last, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> cracked the code.</p><p>Not with a password. Jhostynxon ‘‘The Password’’ Garcia plays for the Pirates.</p><p>Something much more basic: the timely home run.</p><p>Ian Happ broke a tie with a three-run home run, only the third three-run homer hit by the Cubs this month. Pinch hitter Michael Conforto followed two batters later with a two-run home run, the decisive blows in a six-run seventh that carried the Cubs to a 10-4 victory over the Pirates before 12,340 at PNC Park on Wednesday night.</p><p>The 10-game losing streak is over. The best chaser to whatever bitter taste might have been left behind? Happ suggested amnesia.</p><p>“Whatever has happened before this point, it doesn’t matter,’’ said Happ, clearly not a member of the “all past is prologue’’ crowd.</p><p>“It’s completely and totally irrelevant. Like, it doesn’t matter that we had two 10-game winning streaks and doesn’t matter that we had a 10-game losing streak. Doesn’t matter at all.</p><p>“So it’s behind us now. We’re moving forward, we’re four games above .500 and we’re in a good spot.’’</p><p>The Cubs are certainly in a much better place than when the day began, one baseball person describing the teamwide funk that had gripped the club as a “cluster of awfulness.”</p><p>Then someone flipped a switch, and awful quickly ceded the field to giddiness up and down the lineup. The Cubs banged out 14 hits, matching the 14 they put up the last time they won a game, 10-5 over the White Sox on May 15 at the Rate.</p><p>Manager Craig Counsell pointed at Pete Crow-Armstrong as the instigator. PCA refused to give in to the high-octane offerings of Pirates starter Bubba Chandler to draw a leadoff walk, fouling off six pitches in a 10-pitch at-bat that ended with him spitting on two pitches just below the zone.</p><p>“Just a great at-bat to lead off the game,’’ Counsell said. “From the pitcher’s perspective, you have a 10-pitch at-bat and [Crow-Armstrong] gets on base, you’re going to have a tough first inning. And then we made it a tough first inning.’’</p><p>Every spot in the lineup produced at least one hit, Michael Busch and Dansby Swanson reached base four times apiece and five players drove in at least a run, with Happ leading the way with a season-high five RBI. The first two came on a bases-loaded single in the first inning off Chandler, the last three when he crushed a first-pitch sweeper from Johan Ramirez that dawdled in the strike zone, driving it deep into the right-field seats.</p><p>Seiya Suzuki then lined a single off Ramirez, leading to his dismissal, and Conforto buried the first offering from Justin Lawrence deep into the right-field seats.</p><p>“It means a lot to add on,’’ said Conforto, who has two pinch-hit home runs, plus the top-of-the-ninth three-run home run in the Rate that nearly spoiled the Sox’ weekend. “The Pirates have been swinging the bat well, so we knew they had come back twice to tie the score, so we had to keep the pedal down.’’</p><p>Even on a team mired in a collective slump, Happ had stood out. In his previous seven games, interrupted by a two-day “mental refresher,” Happ had gone 2-for-27, striking out 13 times. But that doesn’t matter anymore. Or so he says.</p><p>“Honestly,’’ Busch said, “I think we just do such a good job of, no matter how the day went, just flushing it and moving on to the next.</p><p>“I think for us, just continuing to move forward. We know how good we are. We’ve just got to keep that one foot in front of the other.’’</p><p>Only a spoilsport would mention that all-world Paul Skenes is pitching Thursday for the Pirates.</p><bsp-listcarousel entries.title: 15-year-old boy critically wounded in Bronzeville shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy was critically wounded in a shooting early Thursday in Bronzeville on the South Side. </p><p>Around 3:20 a.m., the teen was found on the ground in the 4800 block of South Calumet Avenue with the gunshot wound to the facial area, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Comer Children's Hospital where he was in critical condition, police said. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Texas' Paxton could end up a disaster for Republicans
entries.summary: <p>MAGA Republicans are celebrating today. President Donald Trump’s handpicked candidate beat the establishment candidate in a runoff for the Senate in Texas. But the road ahead is rocky.</p><p>And if I were Sen. John Cornyn today, I’d be pretty peeved.</p><p>Imagine it. You’re a popular incumbent senator who’s never lost an election in 23 years. Over those years you’ve enjoyed as much as a <a class="Link" href="https://texaspolitics.utexas.edu/set/john-cornyn-job-approval-trend#republican-identification" target="_blank" >70% approval rating</a> among Republicans in Texas, your base.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f90000" name="module-f90000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>You’re primaried by the state’s sitting, scandal-ridden attorney general, Ken Paxton, a man who’s been embroiled in legal battles for nearly a decade, has been impeached, and has faced allegations of infidelity, bribery, securities fraud and abuse of power.</p><p>You manage to best him in March — but with neither candidate reaching a 50% threshold, it goes to a runoff.</p><p>Despite voting with Trump 100% of the time, and despite the urging of your Senate Republican colleagues, Trump endorses the other guy, and at the last minute.</p><p>And then the president’s pick wins in a blowout, effectively retiring you come November.</p><p>Such is life in Trump’s Republican Party, where years of good service and loyalty can evaporate overnight, and his fickle whims and bruised ego can decide your fate on a dime.</p><p>Cornyn will join some other recent casualties of Trump’s capricious ire in Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., who could prove to be a fun thorn in Trump’s side until November now that he’s neutered their reelection bids. Along with Sens. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., these beleaguered Republicans could effectively keep Trump from passing legislation, getting war and ballroom funding and confirming judges and Cabinet appointments.</p><p>But that’s not the only reason this gamble on Paxton could end up being a disaster for Republicans.</p><p>Democrats have been trying to turn this seat blue for years, and with the controversial Paxton rather than the safe Cornyn as the nominee, they have their best shot in a long time. Their nominee, James Talarico, is incredibly popular and has raised a ton of money since Trump turned him and Stephen Colbert into resistance heroes over their <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/what-is-the-equal-time-rule-that-colbert-says-led-cbs-to-pull-his-talarico-interview" target="_blank" >late-night interview</a> back in February. Republicans will have to spend millions more than they would have had Cornyn been the nominee, in a midterm cycle that’s already proving more expensive than they’d like.</p><p>Talarico and Democrats, to be clear, know this and are thrilled Paxton got the nomination. They’ll spend their considerable capital painting Paxton as a corrupt and ethically challenged deadbeat who could be indicted in the future, and exploiting the existing rift in the Republican Party created by this ugly primary.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/ken-paxton-runoff-win-texas-senate-james-talarico-11992855" target="_blank" >Polls and prediction markets</a> look promising for Democrats. Polymarket gave Talarico a 47% chance of beating Paxton after Paxton’s Tuesday night win, within striking distance of Paxton’s 54%.</p><p>And an April poll from the Texas Politics project at the University of Texas gave Talarico an eight-point edge over Paxton in a general election matchup.</p><p>If Talarico manages to pull off the unimaginable — the first Democrat to win a statewide election in Texas in more than 30 years — it will be because of Trump’s shortsighted meddling in what could have been a safe Republican seat had Cornyn been the nominee.</p><p>And while Trump’s recent track record of getting his guys elected is inarguably good, he occasionally gets it wrong. See the ghosts of Herschel Walker and Roy Moore in Georgia and Alabama, respectively.</p><p>Strength and prudence are not the same thing. Sure, Trump was powerful and influential enough to get the problematic Paxton over the line in his runoff. But was it a prudent pick? Only time will tell.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d80000" name="module-d80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. entries.title: Democracy works best when everyone has a seat at the table
entries.summary: <p>The first time I walked into a state capitol, I was 10 years old, holding my father’s hand. It was 1968, and he had just been elected as the first Black person to serve in that legislature since Reconstruction. I remember the sense of awe, the promise of democracy and my belief that public service could be a force for good.</p><p>But what I saw inside told a more difficult truth. Every Black worker in that building held a mop or broom, carried food or coffee, or shined shoes. Women were largely confined to clerical roles. The ideals of equality and representation had not yet caught up with reality.</p><p>My father worked to change that. He introduced legislation to end a grotesque and now unthinkable practice: labeling blood by race, forbidding transfusions between Black and white patients. During the debate, a legislator repeatedly used racial slurs on the chamber floor to oppose the bill. It was a moment that made national headlines and revealed how fiercely some resisted even the most basic expressions of human dignity.</p><p>And yet, progress came.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-220000" name="module-220000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>When I returned nearly 25 years later as a newly elected member of the Louisiana Senate, I witnessed a transformed institution. Black lawmakers were no longer anomalies; they were colleagues. Women and people of color were serving in leadership roles across government. There were still deep disagreements, but there was also cooperation. Lawmakers across party lines worked, argued and ultimately governed in ways that moved the state forward. It was not perfect, but it reflected a broader truth: America’s democracy, at its best, bends toward inclusion.</p><p>A few days ago, I returned once again — this time not as a legislator, but as a citizen and civil rights advocate — testifying against a proposed congressional map that reflects the very kind of zero-sum politics that threatens that progress. From where I stood, the debate was not simply about lines on a map. It was about whether we are moving forward as a democracy or slipping backward.</p><p>Across the country, we are seeing political fights that center less on solving problems and more on holding power. Battles over representation have become increasingly partisan, often overshadowing the urgent challenges facing communities: underfunded schools, rising healthcare costs, economic inequality and declining life expectancy in too many regions.</p><p>From my vantage point leading a national civil rights organization, I hear concerns echoed in boardrooms, community forums and policy discussions alike. Investors, business leaders and everyday citizens are asking the same question: Why are so many policymakers focused on political advantage instead of practical solutions? The answer matters, and not just for governance, but for economic growth, public trust and the health of our democracy.</p><p>History offers a cautionary lesson. The leaders who resisted civil rights and inclusion in the mid-20th century are not remembered as defenders of tradition. They are remembered as obstacles to progress. Their decisions delayed opportunity, deepened divisions and left enduring scars.</p><p>We stand at a similar inflection point today.</p><p>At its core, the current debate over representation is not just about maps or seats. It is about whether we believe power should be shared in a diverse democracy — or concentrated in the hands of a few. True democracy requires inclusion. It demands that different communities, across race, geography and political affiliation have a genuine voice in shaping the future.</p><p>That principle should guide our approach to redistricting and beyond.</p><p>We need to step back from zero-sum thinking and return to a more constructive path. That means creating processes that are transparent, inclusive and focused on fairness, not advantage. It means bringing people together to find common ground, even when it is difficult. And it means recognizing that the legitimacy of our democratic institutions depends on public confidence that the rules are not rigged.</p><p>Just because something can be done does not mean it should be done.</p><p>Public service has always required more than ambition. It demands restraint, judgment and a willingness to put the greater good above partisan gain. At the end of the day, the measure of leadership is not simply whether you win, it is whether you advance justice, strengthen institutions and leave your community better than you found it.</p><p>I have seen what is possible when leaders rise to that challenge. I have seen cooperation replace conflict, and progress emerge from compromise. Those moments remind us that democracy is not a static system, it is a shared responsibility.</p><p>When it works best, everyone has a seat at the table.</p><p>The question before us now is not simply how we draw political lines. It is whether we are willing to move forward together, or risk turning back.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2e0000" name="module-2e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Republicans also calling out Trump's corrupt 'Anti-Weaponization Fund'
entries.summary: <p>Last week, Republican senators grilled acting Attorney General Todd Blanche about the $1.8 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund" created by President Donald Trump's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/19/trump-settles-his-own-lawsuit-against-the-irs-for-1-8-billion-of-your-money/" target="_blank" >settlement</a> of his lawsuit against the IRS. About 45 senators attended the meeting, and "at least half of them were blasting the attorney general," Sen. Ted Cruz, R–Texas, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/ted-cruz-senators-screaming-todd-blanche-trump-anti-weaponization-fund-rcna346599" target="_blank" >reported</a>. "They were pissed."</p><p>It is not hard to see why. The lawsuit that provided the pretext for using taxpayer money to compensate purported victims of "lawfare and weaponization" was legally dubious, the fund has nothing to do with Trump's claims against the IRS, and the main beneficiaries are apt to be the president's allies and supporters.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.flsd.706172/gov.uscourts.flsd.706172.1.0_4.pdf" target="_blank" >lawsuit</a> pitted Trump against agencies he oversees, represented by government lawyers who are forbidden, under an <a class="Link" href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/executive-order-14215-ensuring-accountability-for-all-agencies" target="_blank" >executive order</a> that Trump issued in February 2025, to "advance an interpretation of the law" that "contravenes" the president's position. That bizarre situation prompted the federal judge overseeing the case to <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.flsd.706172/gov.uscourts.flsd.706172.41.0_2.pdf" target="_blank" >question</a> whether it involved a genuine controversy between adverse parties, as required for the lawsuit to proceed.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a50000" name="module-a50000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>The lawsuit was provoked by IRS contractor Charles Littlejohn's <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/former-irs-contractor-sentenced-disclosing-tax-return-information-news-organizations" target="_blank" >illegal leaking</a> of Trump's tax returns. But Trump filed his complaint <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/7431" target="_blank" >too late</a>: more than two years after Littlejohn <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2023/10/12/trump-tax-leak-guilty-plea/" target="_blank" >pleaded guilty</a> to what Trump's personal attorney accurately called "an egregious breach."</p><p>According to Trump's May 18 <a class="Link" href="https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28132616-sdfl-settlement-signed/" target="_blank" >settlement agreement</a> with the IRS, Littlejohn's leaks, which included confidential information about <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2023/09/29/trump-tax-leak-charges-littlejohn-irs/" target="_blank" >thousands</a> of wealthy Americans, epitomized Democrats' use of government power to "target individuals, groups, and entities for improper and unlawful political, personal, and/or ideological reasons." Although that is a counterintuitive way to describe the conduct of a rogue contractor who was prosecuted by the Biden administration, it is the only attempt to justify the Anti-Weaponization Fund as a logical result of Trump's litigation.</p><p>It is <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/20/us/politics/trump-fund-explainer.html" target="_blank" >highly unusual</a> for the Justice Department to settle a lawsuit by agreeing to pay people whose grievances are completely unrelated to the plaintiff's claims, which in this case involved the IRS' allegedly lax oversight of its contractors. Such settlements, in fact, are prohibited by a <a class="Link" href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/12/16/2020-27189/prohibition-on-settlement-payments-to-non-governmental-third-parties" target="_blank" >rule</a> that the Justice Department issued during Trump's first term.</p><p>That rule, which Pam Bondi, then the attorney general, <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/ag/media/1388536/dl?inline" target="_blank" >reaffirmed</a> in February 2025, generally prohibits settlement payments to "a non-governmental person or entity that is not a party to the dispute." There are a few limited exceptions, none of which seem to apply in this case.</p><p>Trump's settlement agreement <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/21/the-1-776-billion-in-trumps-anti-weaponization-fund-fits-a-pattern-of-fanciful-figures/" target="_blank" >arbitrarily assigns</a> $1.776 billion to the Anti-Weaponization Fund — a reference to the nation's founding year that it preposterously claims is "based on the projected valuation of future claimants' claims." The five members of the board charged with doling out that money will be appointed by the attorney general and can be removed by the president "without cause" at any time.</p><p>Although the Justice Department <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-anti-weaponization-fund" target="_blank" >says</a> "there are no partisan requirements to file a claim," it seems clear the process will favor Trump's friends. The board, the composition of which is completely subject to Trump's control, will "cease processing claims" a month and a half before he leaves office, and the settlement agreement describes "lawfare and weaponization" as abuses peculiar to Democrats.</p><p>"I am helping others, who were so badly abused by an evil, corrupt, and weaponized Biden Administration, receive, at long last, JUSTICE!" Trump <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/116618545735076530" target="_blank" >explained</a> Friday. Those "others" presumably include the 1,600 or so Trump supporters who were arrested (and later <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/01/21/trumps-blanket-clemency-for-capitol-rioters-excuses-political-violence/" target="_blank" >pardoned</a> by Trump) for participating in the 2021 Capitol riot.</p><p>The prospect that the fund "could potentially compensate someone who assaulted a police officer" is "absurd," Sen. Thom Tillis, R–N.C., <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/republican-defiance-over-anti-weaponization-fund-sets-up-confrontation-with-2026-05-23/" target="_blank" >remarked</a> last week. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R–Ky., likewise <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/house/5892196-senate-house-republican-tension-anti-weaponization-fund/" target="_blank" >said</a> "a slush fund to pay people who assault cops" was "utterly stupid" and "morally wrong."</p><p>"I'm supposed to work out a settlement with myself," Trump <a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/donald-trumps-irs-lawsuit-threatens-justice-system-11475643" target="_blank" >acknowledged</a> a few days after suing the IRS. The upshot of his admitted self-dealing is an arrangement so <a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/donald-trumps-irs-lawsuit-threatens-justice-system-11475643" target="_blank" >brazenly corrupt</a> that even Republicans are having trouble accepting it.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-720000" name="module-720000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Woman's interest in married man seems pretty clear
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I know a guy from work I'll call "Jon." His girlfriend comes over whenever he does. She doesn't seem at all interested in being my friend, but she talks to my husband for hours on end. When I try to have a conversation with her, she ignores me.</p><p>I tried to bond with her. She came over and wanted to cook in my kitchen, but whenever I volunteered to help her, she asked for my husband to help her instead. She sits by him any chance she can get and tries to make these inside jokes with him. It's beginning to upset me because she acts like I don't exist. It makes me feel like I'm a third wheel in my own home.</p><p>What's worse is Jon doesn't say anything about it, and she ignores him as well. Now she's talking about moving two minutes away from our house and is actively looking for places. I don't know what to do because we are good friends with Jon. — <i>UNCOMFORTABLE IN WEST VIRGINIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNCOMFORTABLE:</b> Enough is enough. Have you discussed this with your husband? If you haven't, start now. Point out that Jon's girlfriend appears to have a super-sized crush on him to the point that she ignores that the two of you are a couple, and the way she treats Jon is insulting and disrespectful. Then tell your spouse you no longer want that woman in your home or even in your neighborhood. If he's afraid to speak up, then you will have to do it. Start by telling Jon you don't want her around and why.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am worried about my 26-year-old son, "Caleb." He's severely overweight. Let me be clear: I love him regardless of his weight, but I think he binge eats to cope with anxiety and depression. A mutual love of eating was how my son and his late mom bonded.</p><p>For example, when his favorite TV show ended its run, Caleb ate three pizzas in one sitting to celebrate the finale. Another time, he ate an entire box of brownies in less than 30 minutes "just to see if he could." When I suggest healthier options for his diet, or maybe that he should eat less, he says sarcastic things like "vegetables are poison" and "let piggy eat his slop."</p><p>Caleb rarely leaves his room in the basement, and he lost touch with his few friends a long time ago. My son is emotionally immature, so it's hard to talk about this with him. I just want my boy to be healthy and happy. How do I get through to him? — <i>WORRIED DAD IN VIRGINIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DAD:</b> Stop lecturing Caleb about his diet because, clearly, it isn't working. At 26, your son is no longer a boy. He's a grown man living in his father's basement. If he doesn't have a job, insist he get one now. It will get him out of his room on a regular basis and perhaps give him some self-esteem. Some discussions about what he plans to do with his life once he is independent might be helpful, as would some sessions with a licensed mental health professional to address his emotional problems.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>To receive a collection of Abby's most memorable — and most frequently requested — poems and essays, send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby — Keepers Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: A new program brings performances to kids in Chicago-area hospitals
entries.summary: <p>Northwestern University theater major Laura Fajardo-Riascos warms up her voice as her classmate, Kennedy Naseem, strums on a ukulele. The duo is sitting in a colorful playroom on the 17th floor of Lurie Children’s Hospital in Streeterville.</p><p>They’re here to put on an interactive show for the kids in this unit, but whether they’ll have an audience all depends on how the young patients are feeling this afternoon in May.</p><p>Fajardo-Riascos and Naseem are among 10 students enrolled in a Northwestern class this spring that is bringing playful, small-scale theater to an unlikely setting: Chicago’s pediatric hospitals. The show, “Let’s Go Camping!,” was developed in part by their professor, Elizabeth Brendel Horn, while she was still working in Florida. entries.title: Why Michelin-starred Atelier closed its doors in Lincoln Square
entries.summary: <p>The Michelin-starred Atelier abruptly closed its doors last week despite its owner's efforts to make it more visible and appeal to more casual diners.</p><p>The eatery with connections to award-winning chefs Christian Hunter and Iliana Regan had just relocated in October to a larger space at 4544 N. Western Ave. and added a bar menu with small plates for customers seeking a more casual dining experience. But the restaurant struggled to sustain its operations<b>. </b></p><p>“We weren't able to get enough people through the door,” owner Tim Lacey said in an email to the Sun-Times. “The reservations just weren't coming in.”</p><p>Lacey opened Atelier in 2023 at 4835 N. Western Ave., previously home to Regan's fine dining restaurant and neighborhood staple Elizabeth. He hired executive chef Christian Hunter, who curated a tasting menu that featured ingredients from Midwestern farms and drew influences from a diverse slate of cultural cuisines. </p><p>Under Hunter’s direction, the restaurant received a Michelin star within the first year. In 2024, Bradyn Kawcak took over as executive chef when Hunter left to start his own concept.</p><p>The closure comes amid industry-wide economic challenges, brought on by inflation. Though the shuttering of Atelier follows the recent closures of two other neighborhood fixtures, Gather and Cafe Selmarie, business leaders say Lincoln Square’s dining scene continues to attract diners and new restaurant operators.</p><p>“While the restaurant industry as a whole is struggling with rising cost of food, rent, wages, taxes, licensing, permitting and inflation, we are fortunate in Lincoln Square to maintain a vibrant dining community," Rudy Flores, president and CEO of Lincoln Square Ravenswood Chamber of Commerce, said in a statement to the Sun-Times.</p><p>"While it is always disappointing to see a restaurant close, especially an acclaimed establishment like Atelier, the reality is that the restaurant industry remains one of the most challenging industries in which to operate profitably, particularly for independent operators who are not part of larger restaurant groups,” the statement continued.</p><p>Flores said in the statement that the neighborhood has minimal restaurant vacancies, and is currently awaiting new openings, such as Zimi’s Pizza in the former 016 Restaurant space. And this year, the new Ardor by Chance opened in the previous Carbon Arc adjacent to the Davis Theater."</p><p>When asked if it was more difficult for a fine dining restaurant to flourish in a neighborhood such as Lincoln Square compared to Downtown, Lacey said he didn’t know. But he tried to make Atelier more approachable by adding options beyond the tasting menu.</p><p>“Our aim was for people to be able to come in and have a bite without having to commit to the tasting menu, and draw more spur-of-the-moment diners as a way to make the restaurant more accessible,” Lacey said.</p><p>Both executive chef Bradyn Kawcak and beverage director Ali Martin announced their departures on May 17 on Instagram.</p><p>“I couldn’t be more grateful to everyone who has helped me along this journey,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DYdBtJ3RCSm/" target="_blank" ><u>Kawcak wrote</u></a>. “Building a team of passionate chefs over the past few years has been the biggest honor of my career thus far. There would be no awards without your hard work. I hate to abruptly end this journey after so much hard work, but I’m excited for the next chapter.”</p><p>Martin told the Sun-Times that she was proud of the community Atelier created.</p><p>“The support from former guests has been moving and the strength of the staff to be here for each other is inspiring,” she wrote in an Instagram message. ”I feel truly blessed to have been able to work with such talented folks and call them my friends. They are what made the restaurant, I’m so sad we don’t get to do it anymore."</p><p>Reflecting on his time at Atelier, former chef and Kentucky native Christian Hunter told the Sun-Times that the role was an opportunity to gain experience in the Chicago market. He said he never expected to win a Michelin star.</p><p>“The only thing I told my team was, we have a high standard that we have to hold ourselves to,” he said. “I was very surprised. It was a struggle doing that sort of menu in Chicago as an unknown chef for nine months, but thanks a lot to the staff that we had, we were lucky enough to be awarded.”</p><p>Hunter cited the restaurant’s “good bones,” or previous reputation as Elizabeth, for helping to garner acceptance in the community.</p><p>“You have to win your neighborhood over,” he said. “If you have a really big-name person or group, you're ahead of the game, but no matter what restaurant you open, your neighborhood has to support you first. Otherwise, nobody's going to know where to travel to come see you.”</p><p>Following his departure from Atelier, Hunter planned to start a seafood bar in Time Out Market before the food hall closed in January. Now, he is working to open Hooligan as a bistro at a to-be-announced location in Logan Square.</p><p>“Nobody wants to hear that a restaurant has closed,” he said of Atelier. “That's people losing jobs, that's a small little ecosystem that just disappears. So, it's very sad to hear.”<br></p>

entries.title: 'Broadview 6' may tap Trump's $1.8B 'anti-weaponization fund' after feds' conduct tanked case
entries.summary: <p>Announcing President Donald Trump’s new $1.776 billion<b> </b>fund<b> </b>for people targeted through “lawfare”<b> </b>in the nation’s courts, acting<b> </b>Attorney<b> </b>General<b> </b>Todd<b> </b>Blanche<b> </b>insisted “the machinery of government should never be weaponized against any American.”</p><p>Three days later,<b> </b>a federal judge in Chicago revealed that an indictment against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters was the result of alleged misconduct by prosecutors — conduct that left her “incredibly shocked.”</p><p>The defendants, known as the “Broadview Six,” are largely involved in Democratic politics in Chicago. But now, their attorneys say they might apply for relief under Trump’s new “anti-weaponization fund” after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >the case was dismissed</a>.</p><p>“You want an example of weaponization?” Christopher<b> </b>Parente, one of their defense attorneys,<b> </b>told reporters when charges were dropped on May 21. “You’ve got prosecutors going into the grand jury targeting political candidates and political figures improperly. These guys should be Exhibit 1.”</p><p>It’s highly unlikely the six protesters, including progressive<b> </b>former congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, are the intended targets of what critics are calling a “slush fund” for Trump’s allies.</p><p>Still, their application could serve as a test of the fund’s purportedly nonpartisan nature.</p><p>It’s also possible that, if they accept money from the Trump fund, they’d be giving up any relief they might secure in a federal courtroom down the road. Anyone who chooses to do so, records show, “must forgo all other relief, including judicial relief.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-510000" name="image-510000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5697d2b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7680x4310+0+405/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2F12%2F485ad4d84438970fc34c90326678%2F2254308915.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b7078e2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7680x4310+0+405/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2F12%2F485ad4d84438970fc34c90326678%2F2254308915.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/23e2907/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7680x4310+0+405/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7c%2F12%2F485ad4d84438970fc34c90326678%2F2254308915.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="U.S. President Donald Trump does a little dance after delivering remarks at the House Republican Party member retreat at the Kennedy Center in Washington, DC, on January 6, 2026. The Trumps also agreed to drop two separate administration claims against the federal government.</p><p>The fund will be overseen by five commissioners appointed by Blanche, one of whom will be selected in consultation with congressional leadership. Trump will have the authority to fire any of them.</p><p>“The use of government power to target individuals or entities for improper and unlawful political, personal, or ideological reasons should not be tolerated by any Administration,” Trent McCotter, an official in the Department of Justice, wrote in a statement announcing the fund.</p><p>The feds have provided few additional details on how the fund will operate or who exactly will be eligible for compensation. But Blanche told a Senate subcommittee anyone can apply regardless of political affiliation. </p><p>Michael Caputo, a longtime Trump ally who served as a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services during his first term, appears to have submitted the first known claim to the fund.</p><p>Caputo argued he and his family were targeted in the “illegal” Crossfire Hurricane investigation into potential Russian interference in the 2016 election. He’s requesting $2.7 million in restitution and reimbursement from the fund.</p><p>Another prominent ally, MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell, also said he plans to file a claim. And former Proud Boys leader Enrique Tarrio, convicted for his role in the insurrection at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, said he would seek millions.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cc0000" name="image-cc0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/77be42a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4328x2429+0+228/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc1%2Ff0%2F72ac573fa32fb1ccda7208caa5a3%2Fcapitol-riot-america.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/22adb08/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4328x2429+0+228/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc1%2Ff0%2F72ac573fa32fb1ccda7208caa5a3%2Fcapitol-riot-america.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9fa683c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4328x2429+0+228/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc1%2Ff0%2F72ac573fa32fb1ccda7208caa5a3%2Fcapitol-riot-america.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="FILE - Violent insurrectionists loyal to President Donald Trump storm the Capitol, Jan. 6, 2021, in Washington. So have two U.S. Capitol police officers who defended the building, calling the fund the “most brazen act of presidential corruption this century.”</p><p>“President Donald J. Trump has created a $1.776 billion taxpayer-funded slush fund to finance the insurrectionists and paramilitary groups that commit violence in his name,” the lawsuit states.</p><h3><b>What does this mean for the ‘Broadview Six’? </b></h3><p>The Broadview defendants are far from Trump allies.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >The group was charged</a> in the midst of Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration’s pummeling deportation campaign in the Chicago area last year. They were accused of joining a larger group of people who surrounded a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent's vehicle and pushed, scratched and otherwise damaged it outside an ICE facility in suburban Broadview.</p><p>Charged along with Abughazaleh were Oak Park village trustee Brian<b> </b>Straw, then-Cook County Board candidate Catherine<b> </b>“Cat”<b> </b>Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael<b> </b>Rabbitt, musician<b> </b>Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh<b> </b>and<b> </b>Andre<b> </b>Martin, a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff.</p><p>A grand jury indictment accused them of a conspiracy<b> </b>to impede a federal agent, and they each initially faced a maximum sentence of seven years behind bars.</p><p>Charges against Sharp and Walsh were dropped in March. </p><p>Then on May 21, Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros made a rare courtroom appearance<b> </b>and admitted to apparent misconduct by his staff before a grand jury<b> </b>last fall. He announced his office would permanently dismiss all charges against the remaining protesters. </p><p>U.S. District Judge April Perry told lawyers she was "incredibly shocked”<b> </b>by what she saw in a set of grand jury transcripts. “I have never seen the types of prosecutorial behavior before a grand jury that I saw in those transcripts,” Perry said.</p><p>But worst of all, Perry said, the problematic behavior had been redacted out of transcripts given to her by the feds. entries.title: Ahead of meeting Pope Leo, Johnson speaks of ‘evolving’ spirituality and ‘constantly growing in my faith’
entries.summary: <p>About a week before her death on June 9, 1995, while she was getting dressed for a church service, Pastor Wilma Jean Johnson stopped her son Brandon, the sixth of her 10 children, as he was about to leave the family home.</p><p>She had something he needed to know. </p><p>Pastor Johnson’s health had been in decline for some time as she battled congestive heart failure and related complications. Perhaps she knew her time was short. Or maybe it was a mother’s irrepressible intuition about her child.</p><p>“I want you to take care of yourself,” her son, Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson, recalled her saying in a wide-ranging conversation with the Sun-Times late last week about his faith, “evolving” spirituality and how they shape his life as a father, partner and public servant.</p><p>“She said, ‘Don't worry about your father, don't worry about your brothers and sisters; I need you to take care of yourself because I see you standing before thousands of people one day, and you are going to have incredible influence on thousands and thousands of people,’” he said. “And that was it.”</p><p>It was the last encounter Johnson had with his mother. He was a 19-year-old college freshman, home briefly for a Sunday afternoon visit. She was barely 50. Four years earlier, she had collapsed and was diagnosed with a heart condition, and just kept going. Until she couldn’t.</p><p>“I think it was just the prophetic words of my mother,” Johnson, who turned 50 in March, said as he prepared to travel to Vatican City to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/05/26/pope-leo-chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-vatican-visit" >meet Pope Leo XIV </a>in a private audience Thursday. “I mean, she never said I'd be mayor of Chicago,” he laughed. "But in that moment it was clear that whatever it was that my father's mission was, mine would be a little different.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/05/27/mayor-brandon-johnson-pope-leo-vatican-visit-reparations-slavery" >Mayor Johnson will enlist Pope Leo’s support in fight for reparations</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Johnson’s father, the Rev. Andrew Johnson, is an ordained minister in the Church of God in Christ, the largest Pentecostal denomination in the United States. For many years with his wife, Wilma Jean, he pastored Community Center Christian Ministries in Elgin and occasionally foster-parented even more children. To help make ends meet for his large family, he also worked at Elgin Mental Health Center, serving patients on the night shift until he lost his position after being accused — falsely, according to his family — of falling asleep on the job. Money was often tight. The family pulled together to support each other in myriad ways.</p><p>There was an expectation, explicit and implicit, that someday Brandon Johnson would take over the family “business,” stepping up to shepherd the church.</p><p>After Wilma Jean’s death, her son didn’t heed her words. At least not immediately.</p><p>“I ended up leaving school and taking some classes at the community college and came home to help dad and to be of support with my siblings,” he said. "You can try so hard for something to happen or materialize. And it just seems like no matter how hard you try, things don't quite ever really settle.”</p><p></p><p>“And I think once I got married [in 1998] and really begin to feel this call to not just take care of myself, but really begin to spend time in prayer, thinking about when that mirror is put up against you and God begins to show you who you are — how do I truly fulfill the purpose that God has in my life that [is] gonna ultimately bring him glory?” Johnson said. “I just began to pursue that calling and that purpose. And I think as I became closer and closer to fulfilling that purpose … it really began to just resonate that there are multiple ways in which you can do ministry. And mine would be through public education and public advocacy that would inevitably lead to me running one of the largest economies in the entire world.”</p><h3>A connection with the Holy Spirit</h3><p>That conversation with his mother, Johnson said, is one of the times he felt he’d had an encounter with the Holy Spirit. It’s not a common topic for most politicians to explore publicly, but Johnson consistently has spoken openly about his spiritual life and beliefs since entering the public square.</p><p>It’s something he has in common with the Chicagoan he’s expected to meet with in the Vatican Apostolic Library Thursday: <a class="Link" Celebrated 50 days after Easter, Pentecost commemorates the Holy Spirit descending on Jesus’ apostles and other followers in a great wind and “tongues of fire” in Jerusalem, according to the biblical account in the Book of Acts, enabling them to preach the gospel to the world. </p><p>“The Holy Spirit opens the door of our heart, helping us to overcome resistance, selfishness, mistrust and prejudice, while enabling us to live as children of God and brothers and sisters to one another,” the pope said. </p><p>Speaking Sunday during a send-off event at Peach’s Restaurant in Bronzeville on the South Side, Johnson, who is leading a delegation of Chicago business, civic, education, and faith leaders to the Vatican, wished those gathered “Happy Pentecost!”</p><p>“I need your prayers,” Johnson continued. “Our city, our state, our country, our world — we need prayer, but I also know that even if we walk by faith, prayer without works is [dead], but we are alive and well in Chicago, aren't we? But it’s also a serious spiritual statement.</p><p>When 133 cardinals gathered in the Vatican’s Sistine Chapel in May 2025 for a conclave to elect the successor to Pope Francis — who turned out to be Cardinal Robert Prevost of Dolton — they began by asking the Holy Spirit to guide them. “Veni Creator Spiritus,” they sang in Latin, meaning “Come, creator Spirit.”</p><h3>Life as a Pentecostal</h3><p>As a lifelong Pentecostal Christian, Johnson is well acquainted with the Holy Spirit. Generally speaking, Pentecostals believe in the ongoing, supernatural presence of the “third person” of the Trinity (i.e. “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit/Holy Ghost”) and that it actively participates in and can shape the daily lives of Christians even today. Sometimes known as the “baptism of the spirit” or “second baptism,” many Pentecostals believe it to be an experience separate from salvation, one often accompanied by “speaking in tongues” or other “gifts of the spirit” such as prophecy and healing.</p><p>Johnson vividly remembers what he describes as his first “encounter” with the Holy Spirit when he was in grade school.</p><p>“It was pretty early in my life — around 9 or 10 years old,” he began. “It was customary for us to spend time on the altar, to really seek God's presence and his spirit to be that comforting force that the Bible promises us, that the Holy Spirit will never leave us or forsake us and will be with us always, even to the end of the age.</p><p>“I think I just learned early in life that if you seek you'll find, and I had a desire to want to live a life that would be acceptable in the eyesight of God. To be of service, I think is probably the best way I can describe it,” he continued. “And I think I learned and discovered early … that there was a specific plan and purpose that God had for my life. And that was to be a life of service to humanity. And that's when I really felt God's presence in his Holy Spirit, you know, really comfort me and confirm that this was what I was supposed to do.”</p><p>Does he remember how it felt, that first encounter with the Holy Spirit on the altar as a child?</p><p>“I remember feeling just protected and safe and that I was as OK as I've ever felt in my life,” he said.</p><h3>Moments of a spiritual presence</h3><p>Are there other moments when he’s felt a similar spiritual presence in his life?</p><p>“Yes — I could think of the birth of my children,” he said, referring to Owen, Ethan and Braedyn I knew God was there,” he said, chuckling as he recalled his first day teaching at Jenner Academy Elementary in Cabrini-Green nearly 20 years ago.</p><p>“I could think of difficult times: When my mother passed away, I knew God and his presence was there. When [I heard] the news about my father, who is in a second or third phase of Alzheimer's. … And how every, every now and then, he'll just give us a little glimmer, and you can just … you see dad. He just sort of peeks out. And he just kind of — for a quick moment — he has a memory and is present,” he said. “Sometimes you believe, you want to believe because you’re desperate, and to hear someone else say that no, that is a real experience — that’s how I know that God is present.”</p><p>How does the mayor describe himself spiritually now?</p><p>“Evolving,” he said. “I mean, constantly growing in my faith as this incredible journey of this faith walk is to believe in the things that have not yet been seen. … And I’m evolving as a husband, which is the best way to model my life after Christ, to love my wife as Christ loves the church. And then, of course, as a parent, to not provoke my children to wrath.”</p><p>And how’s that going?</p><p>“I wanna know where the scripture is about children not provoking their parents to wrath!” he said, laughing again.</p><p>“And then finally, to love your neighbor as yourself. That’s a constant evolution. I think it means not to live in fear. I believe that's why some people struggle with that — when you live in fear. … The many times in the Bible where it says, ‘do not be afraid,’ that's a regular command. And I believe that the fear of the unknown, the fear of others or something else or the fear of losing is why I believe that people struggle to love their neighbor.”</p><p>Earlier this week, Johnson delivered the commencement address at Kenwood Academy High School, where his eldest child, son Owen, who turns 19 in the autumn, was a graduating senior.</p><p>What does Johnson want his children to know — about God, faith, spiritual life — that he didn’t know when he was younger?</p><p>“That they never, ever question how much God loves them,” he said. “I just want them to know that it doesn't matter what they do, that his love will never end. And I say that because I want them to know that as their father, as their parent, that they can always trust me and come to me no matter what. I'm never going to judge them, and that's what I want them to know.</p><p>“I want them to know that they don't have to be afraid, and to know that no matter what, they can always come to me.
